raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 9-year-old boy (whose mother was recently found to be HIV-positive) presented to the hospital with 1 week of right-sided hemiplegia and right-sided facial palsy. Past medical history included psoriasis, diagnosed 4 years prior. His only HIV exposure was perinatal. On exam the patient weighed 22 kilograms, and vitals signs were within normal limits. He was alert and oriented with a normal level of consciousness and responded appropriately to questions. His speech was slowed and slurred, but this was his baseline according to his mother. He had right-sided facial palsy and right-sided tongue deviation; otherwise cranial nerves were intact. The boy had 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and 4/5 strength in the right lower extremity. Left-sided strength was 5/5. The patient was able to walk with limited difficulty. Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ and 3+ throughout. Babinski's sign showed dorsiflexion of the right 1st toe. Sensation was intact throughout. The patient also had clusters of 1-2 mm skin colored papules on his forehead and left cheek in addition to diffuse mild psoriatic scaling. Immunizations were up to date. The patient was admitted for a workup of these symptoms.
Laboratory studies showed complete blood count: hematocrit 31.6%, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 5000 cells/muL (N 41%, L 35%, E 12%, M 6%, B 1%, atypical L 1%), and 157 000 platelets/muL. HIV-antibody test was positive with a CD4 T-cell 0.21% (4 cells/muL) and plasma HIV RNA virus of 185 976 copies/mL (log 5.27). Tests for Cryptococcus antigen, Toxoplasmosis antigen, Ebstein Barr virus IgG and IgM, Cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, Hepes Simplex virus polymerase chain reaction (PCR), Japanese encephalitis as well as cultures for tuberculosis and fungi (plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, CSF) were all negative. Plasma and CSF samples were positive for JCV by real time PCR with a plasma RNA level of 226 copies/mL.
Three days after admission a brain computerized tomography (CT) scan was performed and showed frond-like hypodense lesion at the left frontal lobe with mild effacement of the left frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) regimen was subsequently started 10 days after admission, consisting of GPOvir-Z (coformulated zidovudine 250 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, and nevirapine 200 mg). Clinically, the patient deteriorated during the 1st and 2nd weeks of HAART with fever and increased right leg weakness, but immunologic and virologic improvement was seen (CD4 T-cell count 0.8%, 10 cells/muL, and a plasma HIV RNA viral level of 26 532 copies/mL, log 4.42). CT (Figure 1) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; Figure 2) scans were subsequently performed. The scans showed progressive of white matter lesions with asymmetrical deep and subcortical white matter lesions over the left frontotemporoparietal region and the right frontal lobe. The lesion on the left hemisphere involved internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, and genu of corpus callosum and anterior cerebellar hemisphere. There were no enhanced areas after the contrast study.
The patient was discharged 7 weeks after the first admission. Upon discharge he was able to walk with assistance, but was unable to speak.
The patient was readmitted one day after discharge due to autonomic nervous system dysfunction (nausea, vomiting, and loss of bowel and bladder tone). Deep tendon reflexes were 4+ throughout, and Babinski was positive bilaterally. Continued improvement of immunologic (CD4 T-cell count 2.0%, 30 cells/muL) and virologic (HIV RNA level 3220 copies/mL, log 3.51) measures were seen. Due to progressive neurologic symptoms HAART was ceased. The second MRI (Figure 3) scan was performed and showed a progressive lesion in the same regions as described in the previous MRI, but also found new lesions over the midbrain, pons, and medulla predominantly on the left. The patient was discharged approximately 3 weeks after admission.
The patient was readmitted 1 month later (100 days after onset of symptoms). Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) was suspected, and the boy was treated with methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) for 5 days. Despite HAART suspension and administration of steroids, his clinical symptoms worsened. The third MRI (Figure 4) scan showed new lesions in the regions of the right brainstem and right hemisphere with gyral enhancement. The patient's mother refused further treatment, he was discharged home, and he subsequently died 1 year later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy presenting with a 1-week history of right-sided hemiplegia and right-sided facial palsy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute progressive weakness of the right upper and lower extremities and right facial droop over a 1-week period. He had a baseline of slowed and slurred speech according to his mother. Ten days after admission, he was started on combination antiretroviral therapy; during the 1st and 2nd weeks of therapy, he experienced clinical deterioration with fever and worsening right leg weakness despite virologic and immunologic improvement. He was discharged after 7 weeks, but readmitted one day later with autonomic nervous system dysfunction (nausea, vomiting, and urinary and fecal incontinence), and again at 100 days with progressive neurocognitive decline.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of psoriasis diagnosed 4 years prior. Perinatal exposure to maternal retroviral infection (mother recently tested positive for retroviral disease). Immunizations up to date.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right-sided weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, mild psoriatic scaling; later positive for nausea, vomiting, and bowel and bladder incontinence; negative for sensory loss or seizures. Home medications: unmentioned. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Weight: 22 kg; vital signs: within normal limits on admission. Mental status: alert and oriented with normal level of consciousness, responding appropriately; speech slowed and slurred (baseline). Cranial nerves: right-sided facial palsy and rightward tongue deviation; other cranial nerves intact. Motor: right upper extremity strength 3/5, right lower extremity strength 4/5, left-sided strength 5/5; ambulatory with limited difficulty. Reflexes: deep tendon reflexes 2+ to 3+ throughout (escalating to 4+ on second admission); Babinski sign: dorsiflexion of the right 1st toe (bilateral on readmission). Sensory: intact throughout. Dermatologic: clusters of 1-2 mm skin-colored papules on forehead and left cheek, with diffuse mild psoriatic scaling.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: hematocrit 31.6%, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 5,000 cells/mcL (neutrophils 41%, lymphocytes 35%, eosinophils 12%, monocytes 6%, basophils 1%, atypical lymphocytes 1%), platelets 157,000 cells/mcL. Plasma and CSF tests: negative for Cryptococcus antigen, Toxoplasma antigen, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG and IgM, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG and IgM, Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) PCR, and Japanese encephalitis virus; plasma and CSF cultures for fungi and Mycobacterium tuberculosis: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (day 3): frond-like hypodense lesion in left frontal lobe with mild effacement of the left frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Repeat brain CT and MRI: progressive asymmetrical deep and subcortical white matter lesions over the left frontotemporoparietal region and right frontal lobe, involving left internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, genu of corpus callosum, and anterior cerebellar hemisphere, without contrast enhancement. Second MRI: progressive lesions in previously described areas with new lesions in left midbrain, pons, and medulla. Third MRI (day 100): new lesions in right brainstem and right cerebral hemisphere with gyral enhancement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) complicated by PML-Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (PML-IRIS) in a child with perinatally acquired advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS. Confirmatory testing: HIV-antibody test positive, initial CD4+ T-cell count 0.21% (4 cells/mcL), plasma HIV RNA 185,976 copies/mL (5.27 log10 copies/mL); JC virus (JCV) confirmed positive by real-time PCR in both CSF and plasma (plasma viral load 226 copies/mL). Alternative etiologies (tuberculosis, fungal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV, EBV, HSV, Japanese encephalitis) excluded by negative serology, PCR, and cultures. Management & Outcome: Initiated on HAART (GPOvir-Z: zidovudine 250 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, and nevirapine 200 mg) on day 10. Experienced paradoxical clinical deterioration despite virologic/immunologic response (CD4 rising to 0.8% [10 cells/mcL] and 2.0% [30 cells/mcL]; viral load declining to 26,532 copies/mL and 3,220 copies/mL). HAART was discontinued due to progressive neurotoxicity, and methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for 5 days) was administered for suspected IRIS. Neurologic deficits worsened progressively; palliative discharge was provided, and the patient died 1 year later.
